newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ govt says secret deals impossible today.
newsitem.headline: NZ govt says secret deals impossible today.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Jan 3 - A secret deal 30 years ago in which Australia helped bail New Zealand out of economic difficulty after the 1966 election could not happen now without the public knowing about it, the New Zealand Press Association quoted duty minister Max Bradford as saying.
Bradford said the deal was made during an era governed by the Official Secrets Act, which kept details of even the most trivial matters secret.
It had been in a period "not all that long after the war" when a lot of things were still done in secrecy, he said.
Papers released from the Australian archives recently show the Holyoake government asked Australia for A$50 million to bail out the economy.
Australia agreed to the loan because of close trans-Tasman relations, but with riders.

Canberra agreed to provide a A$20 million loan -- rather than the maximum $50 million sought by Wellington -- with a standby credit of a further A$10 million to act as a bridging standby in case a new government in Wellington needed to go to the International Monetary Fund.

The revelations have prompted a call by the Alliance for parliamentary control of foreign policy. It says it will promote legislation this year to bring all foreign treaties, conventions and policy commitments to parliament for ratification.
But Bradford said he did not believe such a deal could take place in secret now because of the Official Information Act and more open government.
"I'd be very surprised if it could happen today.
"With any international agreement, such as CER or on defence matters, it's tabled in the house and available for the public to see."
Only highly sensitive, defence matters might be kept secret, Bradford said.
Canberra demanded conditions to ensure that after the 1966 elections, New Zealand would be forced to correct an economy wallowing under rising imports and falling commodity prices.

Australia also sought greater access to the New Zealand market under the new New Zealand-Australia Free Trade Agreement, and agreed to lose money in a bid to secure an order from the Royal New Zealand Air Force for 24 supersonic Mirage jet fighters. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
